source: Royal Government of Cambodia, General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA) / Boosting Food Production Program (PMO), "ខែ្សសង្វាក់ផលិតកម្ម ដំណាំពោតនៅកម្ពុជា" (Corn Production Value Chain in Cambodia), 2017
text:
Post-harvest drying is critical to corn quality. Cobs that are not dried promptly after harvest develop visible white/grey mold growth over the kernels within about 5-6 days if left un-dried -- the source's photo comparison shows healthy golden-yellow dried cobs next to badly mold-affected cobs where kernels are covered in fungal growth and discoloration. This mold both reduces market value and can make the corn unsafe/unfit as animal feed, since feed-quality corn specifically requires being kept dry and free of contamination.

Among 250 surveyed households, only 45% overall reported having enough drying space/facilities: 84 households (34%) said they let corn dry naturally in the field before harvest, and 41 households (16%) said they have to bring corn home to dry it. Of those drying at home, reasons cited included following family custom/tradition (18, 44% of that subgroup), following relative or friend advice (10), for farm-management reasons (7), and because their land is far from home (6). For those who dry cobs, methods include drying whole cobs (250 households, 100%), shelling and drying loose kernels (47, 20%), spreading on tarps/mats (36, 14%), or using solar/mechanical drying platforms (16, 6%).
